summary: GrothendieckEulerForms, Part II: a depth-first checkpoint for ring exterior operations, componentwise determinant, the first gamma-filtration steps, and Dedekind Steinitz/rank–Pic classification. Fifty declaration plans use the existing categorical K₀ and Pic carriers. The four-layer scope remains partial: no source-complete or implementation claim is made.

nodes.title: Exterior powers preserve projectivity
nodes.statement: For any projective R-module M and n ≥ 0, Λⁿ_R M is projective. Finiteness of M is not needed for this assertion. For finite M, the existing exteriorPower.instFinite supplies finiteness separately.
hypotheses: R is a commutative unital ring; the zero ring is allowed.
proofSteps: Choose a free module F and maps i:M→F and s:F→M with si=id using Projective.iff_split.
Apply exteriorPower.map to i and s. The baseline composition and identity formulas give a retraction of ΛⁿF onto ΛⁿM.
Use exteriorPower.instFree for ΛⁿF and Projective.of_split. This argument works in all characteristics and never divides by n!.
acceptance: For R=ℤ/2ℤ and n=2 the assertion still holds; no antisymmetrization denominator is allowed.
The n=0 and n=1 cases agree with the baseline zeroEquiv and oneEquiv.

sources.match: Provides the projectivity assertion; the retract proof sharpens the stated finite-projective application using the pinned functorial API.

nodes.title: Tensor closure of finite projectives
nodes.statement: The existing object property finiteProjectiveModules R contains the tensor unit and is closed under the existing ModuleCat tensor product. Hence its full subcategory inherits the existing symmetric monoidal, monoidal preadditive structure, and the baseline SplitK0 commutative ring applies.
hypotheses: R is a commutative unital ring; the zero ring is allowed.
proofSteps: The unit R is finite free. If M and N are generated by finite sets, their pairwise pure tensors generate M⊗N, by tensor-product induction.
Apply Module.Projective.tensorProduct; package the two closure facts as ObjectProperty.IsMonoidal.
Use the existing full-subcategory restriction and SplitK0 ring instances, including of_mul_of. Do not build a second Grothendieck ring presentation.
acceptance: The canonical split/exact comparison sends this tensor product to the same object class.

sources.match: The new declaration supplies only the finite-projective closure needed to instantiate the existing categorical construction.

nodes.title: Exterior powers of a direct sum
nodes.statement: For arbitrary R-modules M,N and n≥0 there is an R-linear isomorphism Λⁿ(M⊕N) ≅ ⨁_{i=0}ⁿ ΛⁱM⊗Λⁿ⁻ⁱN. The summand (i,n−i) maps by exterior multiplication, placing the M factors before the N factors.
hypotheses: R is a commutative unital ring; the zero ring is allowed.
proofSteps: Construct the map from each tensor summand using the universal alternating maps and the inclusions into M⊕N; exterior multiplication concatenates the M and N lists.
Construct the inverse on a wedge of pairs by multilinearly expanding into subsets of positions. Use the shuffle sign to move M positions before N positions.

In the two composites, the universal alternating relations eliminate repeated positions and the signed shuffle expansion gives the identity. This is an integral identity, with no factorial denominator.
acceptance: For n=1 the isomorphism is the standard M⊕N decomposition.
For M=N=R and n=2 the unique mixed term is R and its generator is (1,0)∧(0,1).

sources.match: The displayed direct-sum decomposition supplies the relation used by virtual λ-operations.

nodes.title: Exterior-class convolution
nodes.statement: For finite projectives P,Q, [Λⁿ(P⊕Q)] = Σ_{i=0}ⁿ [ΛⁱP]·[Λⁿ⁻ⁱQ] in the existing ring K₀(R).
hypotheses: R is a commutative unital ring; the zero ring is allowed.
proofSteps: All summands are finite projective by the exterior-power lemma and tensor closure.
Apply class invariance to exterior-direct-sum, then iterate the existing biproduct relation and use of_mul_of on every term.
acceptance: The statement retains the displayed hypotheses and the actual module/K₀ carriers.

sources.match: Object-level input to the group-completion argument.

nodes.title: Total exterior operation on virtual classes
nodes.statement: Define λₜ:K₀(R)→(1+tK₀(R)[[t]], multiplication) as the unique additive-to-multiplicative homomorphism taking [P] to Σₙ[ΛⁿP]tⁿ. Represent its target inside the units of the existing power-series ring, with constant term 1. Negative virtual classes use the inverse power series; they are not truncated exterior polynomials.
hypotheses: R is a commutative unital ring; the zero ring is allowed.
proofSteps: The object series has constant coefficient [R]=1, hence is a unit. Exterior functoriality makes it invariant under isomorphism.
exterior-class-sum and the power-series Cauchy-product coefficient formula show that a biproduct maps to a product.
Apply the baseline SplitK0 universal property with the additive form of the multiplicative unit group. The inverse formula and uniqueness follow from the additive-group homomorphism laws.
acceptance: The statement retains the displayed hypotheses and the actual module/K₀ carriers.

nodes.title: Exterior convolution for virtual sums
nodes.statement: For every x,y∈K₀(R) and n≥0, λⁿ(x+y)=Σ_{i=0}ⁿ λⁱ(x)λⁿ⁻ⁱ(y).
hypotheses: R is a commutative unital ring; the zero ring is allowed.
proofSteps: The total operation sends addition to multiplication. Take the n-th coefficient and apply the finite Cauchy-product formula.
acceptance: λ²(x+y)=λ²x+xy+λ²y, using λ⁰=1 and λ¹=id.

nodes.statement: For n>0, λⁿ(−x)=−Σ_{i=0}^{n−1} λⁿ⁻ⁱ(x)λⁱ(−x). The recursion is integral and determines the negative operation from lower coefficients.
hypotheses: R is a commutative unital ring; the zero ring is allowed.
proofSteps: Apply lambda-add to x+(−x)=0. The n-th coefficient is zero.
Separate the i=n term containing λ⁰(x)=1 and rearrange. Reindex the remaining finite sum.
acceptance: For n=1, λ¹(−x)=−x.
For n=2, λ²(−x)=x²−λ²(x).

nodes.title: Exterior coefficients of finite free modules
nodes.statement: For all m,n≥0, λⁿ(m[R])=choose(m,n)[R].
hypotheses: R is a commutative unital ring; the zero ring is allowed.
proofSteps: Identify m[R] with the class of R^m using the existing biproduct relation.
Use the finite-free exterior basis and its binomial cardinality, then identify the resulting free-module class. Handle the zero ring separately, where all classes vanish.

sources.match: Integral binomial normalization on free projectives.

nodes.title: Exterior powers commute with scalar extension
nodes.statement: For a commutative R-algebra S, every R-module M and n≥0, S⊗RΛⁿ_RM ≅ Λⁿ_S(S⊗RM). The comparison sends 1⊗(m₁∧…∧mₙ) to (1⊗m₁)∧…∧(1⊗mₙ).
hypotheses: R is a commutative unital ring; the zero ring is allowed.
proofSteps: Apply the alternating-map universal property and extension-of-scalars universal property to construct the indicated comparison.
For an S-module N, both sides represent R-multilinear alternating maps Mⁿ→N. The two universal factorizations give mutually inverse maps; uniqueness proves naturality.
acceptance: Specializing to n=0 gives S⊗R R≅S.
Specializing to n=1 gives the identity base-change comparison.

sources.match: The base-change statement is valid for all modules and all commutative algebra maps.

nodes.title: The top exterior power is invertible
nodes.statement: If P is a finite projective R-module with rankAtStalk(P,p)=n for every prime p, then ΛⁿP is invertible in the existing Module.Invertible sense.
hypotheses: R is a commutative unital ring; the zero ring is allowed.
proofSteps: Use the finite-projective local-freeness and constant-rank interface supplied by Z.2. The base-change comparison and free exterior basis show that ΛⁿP is locally free of rank one.

By projective-dual-base-change, localizing the dual evaluation map identifies it with evaluation for a free rank-one module. That evaluation is an isomorphism. Apply bijective_of_isLocalized_maximal and package its inverse as a linear equivalence.
Package this actual dual evaluation equivalence as the existing Module.Invertible structure. Local freeness is used only through the explicit Z.2 supplier contract.
acceptance: For a rank-zero finite projective, Λ⁰P=R is invertible.
For a rank-one projective P, its determinant is P.

sources.match: Top exterior degree must use the actual constant rank.

nodes.title: Componentwise determinant of a projective
nodes.statement: For finite projective P, partition Spec R into its finitely many clopen rank fibres U_r. Let R≅∏_rR_r be the corresponding canonical idempotent decomposition and P_r=R_r⊗RP. Define detProjective(P)∈Pic(R) as the class of the R-module ∏_rΛʳ_{R_r}P_r. The rank-zero factor contributes R_r. Refinement of the partition does not change this class.
hypotheses: R is a commutative unital ring; the zero ring is allowed.
proofSteps: Import the clopen rank/idempotent decomposition from Z.2; on each component use constant-rank-top-invertible.
The finite product of these component modules has a tensor inverse given componentwise by their duals. Apply the existing Pic constructor.
Compare two decompositions on their common idempotent refinement using exterior-base-change; regroup the finite products. This proves independence, including ranks which occur on no component.
acceptance: The statement retains the displayed hypotheses and the actual module/K₀ carriers.

sources.match: Uses every rank fibre, without choosing a global rank on disconnected spectra.

nodes.title: Determinant of a direct sum
nodes.statement: For finite projective P,Q, det(P⊕Q)=det(P)⊗det(Q) as invertible-module classes.
hypotheses: R is a commutative unital ring; the zero ring is allowed.
proofSteps: Refine the clopen rank decompositions until P,Q have constant ranks m,n.

Use the exterior-direct-sum formula in degree m+n. All terms except i=m vanish because the corresponding exterior degree exceeds the rank of P or Q; prove that vanishing by the free local model and the local zero-module criterion.
The surviving term is ΛᵐP⊗ΛⁿQ. Reassemble the components and use Pic.mk_tensor.

nodes.title: Surjectivity of the determinant
nodes.statement: Every Pic class is the determinant of its own finite-projective class in K₀. In particular detHom is surjective.
hypotheses: R is a commutative unital ring; the zero ring is allowed.
proofSteps: Represent a Pic element by its existing invertible module. It is finite projective, and determinant-line identifies its determinant with the original Pic element.
acceptance: A nonprincipal invertible ideal remains visible under determinant.

nodes.title: Gamma operations
nodes.statement: For x∈K₀(R), define γ⁰(x)=1 and, for n≥1, γⁿ(x)=λⁿ(x+(n−1)[R]). Equivalently γₜ(x)=λ_{t/(1−t)}(x); the substitution is formal and integral.
hypotheses: R is a commutative unital ring; the zero ring is allowed.
proofSteps: Use coefficient extraction of the substituted power series, or the displayed shifted-coefficient expression. The equivalence of these descriptions is a separate lemma.
acceptance: The statement retains the displayed hypotheses and the actual module/K₀ carriers.

sources.match: The shift uses virtual addition, and is not λⁿ(x) without the shift.

nodes.title: Gamma substitution identity
nodes.statement: For every n≥1, γⁿ(x)=Σ_{j=1}ⁿ choose(n−1,j−1)λʲ(x). Thus Σγⁿ(x)tⁿ=λ_{t/(1−t)}(x).
hypotheses: R is a commutative unital ring; the zero ring is allowed.
proofSteps: Expand λⁿ(x+(n−1)) by lambda-add and use lambda-free on the integer summand.
The j=0 term vanishes and the remaining binomial coefficients are choose(n−1,j−1). These are exactly the coefficients of (t/(1−t))ʲ.
acceptance: For n=2 this recovers γ²(x)=λ²(x)+x.

sources.match: Expanded finite-sum form makes the formal substitution explicit.

nodes.title: First gamma operation
nodes.statement: γ¹(x)=x.
hypotheses: R is a commutative unital ring; the zero ring is allowed.

nodes.title: Gamma convolution
nodes.statement: For all n≥0 and x,y∈K₀(R), γⁿ(x+y)=Σ_{i=0}ⁿγⁱ(x)γⁿ⁻ⁱ(y).
hypotheses: R is a commutative unital ring; the zero ring is allowed.
proofSteps: Substitution t↦t/(1−t) preserves multiplication of power series because the substituted series has zero constant term.
Apply the additive-to-multiplicative property of lambdaTotal and take coefficients. The degree-zero case uses λ⁰=1.
acceptance: The statement retains the displayed hypotheses and the actual module/K₀ carriers.

nodes.title: Augmentation ideal
nodes.statement: Let ρ:K₀(R)→H⁰(Spec R,ℤ) be the virtual rank ring homomorphism supplied by Z.2, normalized by ρ([P])(p)=rankAtStalk(P,p). Define I_R=ker ρ as an ideal of the existing K₀ ring.
hypotheses: R is a commutative unital ring; the zero ring is allowed.
proofSteps: Take the kernel ideal of the specified ring homomorphism. Keep its locally constant function target; neither connectedness nor a single global integer rank is assumed.
acceptance: The statement retains the displayed hypotheses and the actual module/K₀ carriers.

sources.match: The rank kernel is the augmentation ideal used by the γ-filtration.

nodes.title: Rank-zero membership
nodes.statement: x∈I_R if and only if ρ(x)=0 in H⁰(Spec R,ℤ).
hypotheses: R is a commutative unital ring; the zero ring is allowed.
proofSteps: Unfold the kernel ideal.
acceptance: The statement retains the displayed hypotheses and the actual module/K₀ carriers.

sources.match: The kernel membership formula.

nodes.title: Rank of virtual exterior coefficients
nodes.statement: At every prime p and for every virtual class x and n≥0, ρ(λⁿx)(p)=choose(ρ(x)(p),n), with the integral generalized binomial coefficient for an integer upper argument.
hypotheses: R is a commutative unital ring; the zero ring is allowed.
proofSteps: For an actual projective class, localize at p and use the free exterior basis and the normalized virtual rank map.
Apply ρ coefficientwise to lambdaTotal. The object-level identity says the resulting series is (1+t) raised to the local rank.
Multiplication and inversion extend this identity from positive projectives to virtual differences, giving generalized integer binomial coefficients; no rationalization of K₀ is involved.
acceptance: At local rank −1, the coefficient rank is (−1)ⁿ.
At local rank zero, every positive exterior coefficient has rank zero.

sources.match: Extends the source rank compatibility to virtual coefficients via its group-completion argument.

nodes.title: Positive gamma coefficients have rank zero
nodes.statement: If x∈I_R and n>0, then γⁿ(x)∈I_R.
hypotheses: R is a commutative unital ring; the zero ring is allowed.
proofSteps: At every prime, the rank of x+(n−1) is n−1. By rank-lambda the n-th coefficient has rank choose(n−1,n)=0.
Use extensionality of the rank function and augmentation-membership.
acceptance: The statement retains the displayed hypotheses and the actual module/K₀ carriers.

nodes.title: Weighted gamma filtration
nodes.statement: For n≥0, define Fⁿ_γK₀(R) to be the ideal generated by finite products ∏_{j=1}ᵐγ^{k_j}(x_j), where x_j∈I_R, k_j≥1, and Σk_j≥n. Allow the empty product, which occurs only when n=0 and gives F⁰=K₀. This uniform formula also gives F¹=I_R. This is the ideal-generated version; agreement with the source additive-subgroup filtration is an explicit proof gap.
hypotheses: R is a commutative unital ring; the zero ring is allowed.
proofSteps: Use the existing ideal span of the specified set of finite weighted products. The generator data consist of a finite index set, positive natural degrees and elements of the actual augmentation ideal.
acceptance: The statement retains the displayed hypotheses and the actual module/K₀ carriers.

sources.match: The weights are the operation degrees, not the number of factors. The source uses additive subgroup generation. The ideal-span comparison remains open and is not asserted here.

nodes.title: First filtration ideal
nodes.statement: For the normalized virtual rank map, F¹_γ=I_R.
hypotheses: R is a commutative unital ring; the zero ring is allowed.
proofSteps: A positive-weight product has at least one factor, and every positive γ-coefficient of a rank-zero class belongs to I_R by gamma-rank-zero. The ideal-span universal property gives F¹_γ⊆I_R.
For x∈I_R, the one-factor product γ¹(x)=x is a weight-one generator, giving the reverse inclusion.

nodes.title: Dual base change for finite projectives
nodes.statement: For every commutative R-algebra S and finite projective M, there is an S-linear equivalence S⊗RHom_R(M,R) ≅ Hom_S(S⊗RM,S), taking s⊗f to the functional t⊗m ↦ st f(m).
hypotheses: R is a commutative unital ring; the zero ring is allowed.
proofSteps: Commute the tensor factors and apply the existing dualTensorHomEquiv with N=S. This gives an R-linear equivalence with Hom_R(M,S).
Use the scalar-extension adjunction to identify Hom_R(M,S) with Hom_S(S⊗RM,S). The displayed pure-tensor formula shows that the composite and its inverse respect the S-action.
The formula also proves compatibility with dual evaluation, which is the precise local input to the top-exterior determinant proof.
acceptance: For M=R the comparison is the ordinary scalar multiplication functional.
No flatness hypothesis on R→S is imposed.

sources.locator: §3, p.15, dual and tensor closure; p.16, determinant
sources.match: The finite-projective base-change comparison extends the pinned dualTensorHomEquiv; the finite-free-only dual base-change theorem does not suffice on its own.

nodes.title: Exterior powers above local rank vanish
nodes.statement: For finite projective M and n≥0, if rankAtStalk(M,p)<n for every prime p, then ΛⁿM is the zero module.
hypotheses: R is a commutative unital ring; the zero ring is allowed.
proofSteps: Localize at a maximal ideal. The Z.2 local-freeness interface and exterior-base-change identify the localization with the exterior power of a finite free module of rank below n.
Its exterior basis has no n-element subsets, so it is the zero module. Apply the pinned local zero-module criterion.
acceptance: For a rank-one line L, Λ²L=0.
The strict inequality is necessary: Λ⁰0=R for a nonzero ring.

sources.match: The vanishing step is made explicit with its local-rank hypothesis.

nodes.title: Coprime representative of an ideal class
nodes.statement: For nonzero ideals I,J in a Dedekind domain, there is a nonzero integral ideal J′ coprime to I and R-linearly isomorphic to J.
hypotheses: R is a Dedekind domain (commutative and nonzero). Ideals described as invertible are nonzero.
proofSteps: If I=R, use J itself. Otherwise apply the pinned fractional-ideal theorem exists_add_spanSingleton_mul_eq to a=I, b=J and c=R. It gives I+αJ=R inside Frac(R).
The equality implies αJ⊆R. Pull this submodule back along the injective algebra map to obtain an integral ideal J′. The same equality gives I+J′=R.

Since I≠R, α cannot be zero. Multiplication by α is an R-linear equivalence from J to J′: the baseline mem_singleton_mul gives its surjectivity, and cancellation in the fraction field gives injectivity. Thus J′ is nonzero. This proof uses the existing general fractional-ideal approximation theorem and requires no new CRT or valuation-support machinery.
acceptance: When I=R, J itself is a valid representative.
The representative is required to remain nonzero.

sources.locator: Corollary 1.2.11, printed p.5; Lemma 1.2.20 proof, p.9
sources.match: Preserves the isomorphism class while obtaining coprimality.

nodes.title: The coprime ideal sum identity
nodes.statement: For coprime ideals I,J of any commutative ring, I⊕J ≅ R⊕IJ. The map to the first factor is (x,y)↦x+y.
hypotheses: R is a commutative ring; I and J are ideals with I+J=R.
proofSteps: Choose i∈I,j∈J with i+j=1. The sum map f:I⊕J→R has the explicit section r↦(ri,rj).
Its kernel is identified with I∩J by z↦(z,−z). The inverse splitting sends v to (f(v),v−section(f(v))).
Use the pinned equality I∩J=IJ to obtain the displayed isomorphism. This argument does not need Dedekind hypotheses.
acceptance: I=R,J=0 gives R⊕0≅R⊕0.
For I=2ℤ and J=3ℤ the kernel is identified with 6ℤ.

sources.match: The constructive split-kernel argument.

nodes.title: The two-ideal Steinitz identity
nodes.statement: For nonzero ideals I,J of a Dedekind domain R, I⊕J ≅ R⊕IJ.
hypotheses: R is a Dedekind domain (commutative and nonzero). Ideals described as invertible are nonzero.
proofSteps: Choose a coprime J′ and an R-linear equivalence J≅J′. Apply coprime-ideal-sum to I,J′.
Identify each nonzero integral ideal with its image in Frac(R) along the injective algebra map. FractionalIdeal.mk0 and unitsMulEquivSubmodule make those images invertible submodules.

The pinned tensorEquivMul identifies I⊗J with IJ and I⊗J′ with IJ′. Tensor the given equivalence by I and compose these comparisons. This supplies IJ≅IJ′ for an arbitrary module equivalence; no chosen scalar witness is required.
acceptance: For J=R this reduces to swapping the two summands.
For a nonprincipal ideal I, I⊕I⁻¹ is free of rank two after using fractional-ideal representatives.

sources.match: The required rank-two identity, with nonzero ideal hypotheses.

nodes.title: Decomposition into invertible ideals
nodes.statement: Every finite projective P over a Dedekind domain is isomorphic to a finite direct sum of nonzero integral ideals; the empty sum is allowed and represents P=0.
hypotheses: R is a Dedekind domain (commutative and nonzero). Ideals described as invertible are nonzero.
proofSteps: Use the pinned Module.Finite.exists_comp_eq_id_of_projective presentation to embed P in R^N. Induct on N, using the projection onto one coordinate.
If the projection image is zero, P embeds in R^(N−1). Otherwise its image is a nonzero integral ideal I. This ideal is finite and torsion-free, hence projective by the three pinned baseline facts.
Split P→I. The kernel embeds in R^(N−1) and is a direct summand of P, hence finite projective. Apply the induction hypothesis to the kernel and append I. No Bass cancellation theorem is used.
acceptance: The zero module has n=0, with no artificial nonzero ideal.
A nonzero invertible ideal itself gives a one-summand decomposition.

sources.match: Projective ideal summands obtained by coordinate projection and splitting.

nodes.title: Steinitz classification of projectives
nodes.statement: Every finite projective P over a Dedekind domain is either zero or isomorphic to Rⁿ⊕I for some n≥0 and a nonzero invertible ideal I. Its positive rank is n+1. The ideal class of I is determined by det(P).
hypotheses: R is a Dedekind domain (commutative and nonzero). Ideals described as invertible are nonzero.
proofSteps: Start with projective-ideal-summands. If the family is empty the module is zero.
For a nonempty family, repeatedly apply ideal-sum to combine the ideal factors while producing one additional copy of R.

Apply the already specified determinant formulas to identify the resulting ideal class. The rank is obtained after extending to the fraction field, where each nonzero ideal becomes a one-dimensional vector space.
acceptance: The first disjunct handles the actual zero module.
A rank-one nonprincipal ideal lies in the n=0 positive-rank case and is not declared free.

sources.locator: Theorem 1.2.19 and proof, printed pp.9–10; Corollary 1.2.24, p.11
sources.match: State positive rank separately; the proof explicitly handles rank zero before the inductive step.

nodes.title: Additive class formula for tensor products of lines
nodes.statement: Over a Dedekind domain, [L⊗M]=[L]+[M]−[R] for all invertible modules L,M. Equivalently, the product of the two reduced classes [L]−1 and [M]−1 is zero.
hypotheses: R is a Dedekind domain (commutative and nonzero). Ideals described as invertible are nonzero.
proofSteps: Represent L,M by nonzero integral ideals, using the pinned invertible-module-to-ideal comparison. Transport ideal-sum to L⊕M≅R⊕(L⊗M).
Apply the existing biproduct and tensor class relations and rearrange. The equivalent reduced-product formula follows by distributivity.
acceptance: L=M=1 gives [R]=[R]+[R]−[R].
A nontrivial line class can have nonzero reduction while its reduced square is zero.

sources.match: Dedekind specialization proved by the concrete ideal identity, without importing the full dimension-one theorem.

nodes.title: Rank and determinant normal form
nodes.statement: For a finite projective P over a Dedekind domain, [P]=(rank P−1)[R]+[det P], including P=0. Here rank is the fraction-field rank, extended additively to K₀.
hypotheses: R is a Dedekind domain (commutative and nonzero). Ideals described as invertible are nonzero.
The Z.2 rank map is normalized by fraction-field dimension on every projective class.
proofSteps: In the zero case rank(P)=0 and det(P)=1, so the expression is −[R]+[R]=0.
In the positive case Steinitz gives P≅Rⁿ⊕I. The biproduct relation gives [P]=n[R]+[I].
The rank normalization gives rank(P)=n+1, and the determinant formulas identify the Pic class of I with det(P). Use mk_eq_mk_iff to transport the module class.
acceptance: For P=0 the integer coefficient is −1 and the line contribution is +1.
For a rank-one nonprincipal ideal I the formula is [I]=[I], not [I]=1.

sources.match: Explicit inverse formula for the Dedekind special case.

nodes.title: Rank and Picard group classification
nodes.statement: For a Dedekind domain R, rank and determinant give an additive equivalence K₀(R) ≃ ℤ⊕Pic(R). Pic is written multiplicatively. The inverse sends (n,L) to (n−1)[R]+[L], for every integer n, including negative n.
hypotheses: R is a Dedekind domain (commutative and nonzero). Ideals described as invertible are nonzero.
Use the Z.2 rank homomorphism with its fraction-field dimension normalization.
proofSteps: Combine the normalized rank and determinant homomorphisms.
Define the inverse by (n,L)↦(n−1)[R]+[L]. line-class-product proves its additivity; normalized rank and determinant-line prove that the forward composite is the identity.
The reverse composite is an additive endomorphism of K₀. projective-class-normal-form proves the identity on every object class, and the existing universal property proves it globally.
acceptance: The statement retains the displayed hypotheses and the actual module/K₀ carriers.

sources.match: Dedekind domains have connected spectrum, so H⁰ is ℤ.

Keep the early module inputs independent of Z.3 and higher K-theory. For a Dedekind domain, provide the integer-valued specialization normalized by fraction-field dimension.

Instantiate the existing ExactK0 for actual finite locally free sheaves, with the genuine exact structure, and identify the supplier vector-bundle interface.
Establish the precise global finite-resolution hypotheses for K/G comparison on a connected regular Noetherian curve, including the ample-family argument or an appropriately qualified replacement.

Extend the upstream smooth proper/projective divisor/line dictionaries to the full general-curve scope; prove rank/determinant classification and structure, divisor and skyscraper class formulas. Import the origin-dependent elliptic Pic computation from E.2 only for the specialization.
Import the generic pi0 comparison and prove equality of the actual maps on projectives and perfect-complex Euler classes; compare to the existing Cartan map.
Give actual field, integer, product-of-two-fields and nonprincipal-ideal examples, rather than only conditional nontrivial-Pic tests.
Import S.5 for P¹ and prove the rank/degree change of basis (r,d)↦(r+d,−d) relative to (1,O(−1)); import E.2 late for the elliptic origin-dependent test.

gaps.title: Special-lambda splitting without a backward dependency
gaps.detail: Weibel II8.8.1–8.8.3 uses the projective-bundle theorem II8.5 to prove an injective flag-bundle splitting map. Before adding the full special-lambda identities, identify an independently scheduled degree-zero prefix of SchemeKTheoryOperations:S.5 or decompose a separate algebraic proof. Do not add a coarse S.5→Z.3 request if it closes a cycle through early Z.3 operations.

gaps.title: General regular-curve resolution and divisor dictionary
gaps.detail: The source and RS-18 boundary require more than the upstream smooth proper/projective curve APIs. A proof via an ample family from complements of affine opens still needs the exact locally Noetherian, separation and resolution-property hypotheses checked against a primary source. Regularity in arbitrary dimension alone does not supply global vector-bundle resolutions. No curve equivalence is asserted in this checkpoint.

gaps.title: Actual S-integer localization and transfer
gaps.detail: The number-field S-integer localization needs a precise ring isomorphism and ideal-class quotient, using class-group finiteness where principal powers of S-primes are chosen. A valuation overring of an arbitrary Dedekind domain must not be silently identified with an element localization. The finite-flat determinant norm formula and its algebra-determinant factor still need declaration-level proof suppliers.

gaps.title: Agreement with the additive gamma filtration
gaps.detail: The source defines additive subgroups generated by weighted gamma products. This checkpoint packages their ideal span so it can prove ideal multiplication directly. Show that the source additive subgroup is already stable under arbitrary K₀ coefficients, using the clopen rank/idempotent decomposition and compatibility of gamma with restriction to those components. For connected rank, write each coefficient as an integer plus a rank-zero class; for disconnected rank the component argument is essential. Until this comparison is decomposed, do not claim that the chosen ideal span is the source filtration.

sourceIssues.locator: Combined author draft dated 29 August 2013, Theorem II4.10 proof, printed p.98/PDF p.106.
sourceIssues.correction: Use the minimal polynomial in the divisibility assertion; fix k>1 as in E7.
sourceIssues.reason: An annihilating square-free product implies that the minimal polynomial divides that product and proves diagonalizability. It does not constrain eigenvalue multiplicities in the characteristic polynomial: for example, the identity on a two-dimensional space is annihilated by t−1 but has characteristic polynomial (t−1)². The source supplies no one-dimensionality assertion for its weight spaces, and diagonalizability needs only the minimal-polynomial conclusion.
